opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, thanks for having me. I think this is one of the most interesting questions right now, because for a long time the dominant recipe has been: if you want a smarter model, you add more parameters and more data. And that works, but it treats every parameter as doing a relatively fixed, shallow amount of work per token. Each weight gets used once in a forward pass, in a fairly simple multiply-and-add, and then you move on.

What I find compelling is the idea that you can get a lot more out of the same parameters if you let them do more computation, more expressive computation, for each input. One way to think about it is in terms of memory and learning at test time. In a standard Transformer, attention is essentially a very precise but short-term memory: it stores everything in the context and looks it up. The MLP layers are more like long-term, fixed memory, frozen after training. But in a model where some of the layers are themselves learning, where the memory module is updated with a small optimization step as new tokens come in, every parameter is now involved in a more complex process. You're not just reading the weights; you're computing gradients, deciding what is surprising, what to keep, what to forget. That's much more computation per parameter, and it turns out to buy you a lot of expressivity.

And there's a theoretical side to this too. If you look at what kinds of problems these architectures can solve, a fixed-depth Transformer is quite limited in circuit-complexity terms; there are fairly simple state-tracking problems it struggles with unless you make it deeper or let it generate a chain of thought. When you make the recurrence or the memory update more expressive, for instance nonlinear rather than purely linear, or using a deeper memory instead of a single matrix, you can escape some of those limitations without simply scaling up width or depth.

So in a sense, chain-of-thought reasoning is already one form of increasing computation, but it's done in token space, which is expensive and somewhat indirect. What we're exploring is doing more of that computation inside the architecture itself, in the latent space, so the model can effectively think more per token, adapt to the context it's seeing, and use its capacity more efficiently. I think that's a much more parameter-efficient path to smarter models than just making everything bigger.

r001.rationale: The response discusses parameter efficiency compared with scaling models, but does not compare current LLMs’ cost efficiency with humans doing comparable tasks.

r002.rationale: It describes doing more computation inside the architecture so the model can “effectively think more per token.”

r003.rationale: It describes adapting to context as tokens arrive and becoming smarter, but does not clearly state that computing over past data before a token prediction improves next-token prediction quality.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that a parameter is really just stored knowledge, and computation is what you do with that knowledge. Right now, most of our models spend a roughly fixed amount of compute per token regardless of how hard that token is. A Transformer does the same number of operations whether it's predicting "the" after "of" or working through a step in a proof. That's a strange way to allocate resources.

So when I say increasing computation per parameter, I mean a few related things. One is depth of processing at test time: letting the model iterate over its own representations, refine them, take multiple passes over the same weights, instead of a single forward sweep. The same parameters, used more times, can express much more complex functions. There's good theoretical reason to believe this: a fixed-depth network has limited expressivity for certain sequential or compositional problems, but if you can loop or recur, you can simulate much longer computations with a small set of weights.

The second thing is memory. A lot of what we call reasoning is really about keeping track of state across a long context, and the standard attention mechanism handles that by storing everything and then paying quadratic cost to look back. What we've been exploring, with Titans and some follow-up work, is the idea of a neural memory that actually learns at test time. Instead of the context being a passive buffer, the model updates a small set of memory parameters as it reads, based on how surprising each piece of information is. That's computation per parameter in a very literal sense: you're doing gradient-like updates on the fly, so each parameter in the memory module is doing far more work than a frozen weight would.

And the reason I think this makes models smarter rather than just more efficient is that it changes what the model can learn to do. If you give the architecture the ability to spend variable compute, to revisit and revise, to write things into memory and consult them later, then training will discover algorithms that use those abilities. You end up with a system that behaves less like a lookup table and more like something that actually works through a problem. Scaling parameters gives you more knowledge. Scaling compute per parameter gives you more thinking, and I'd argue that's the dimension we've underexploited.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts fixed compute per token with harder and easier tokens, but does not compare LLM cost efficiency with humans performing comparable tasks.

r002.rationale: It describes repeated computation with the same parameters as “more thinking” and as working through a problem.

r003.rationale: It discusses iterative processing and memory, but does not clearly state that doing additional computation over past data before predicting a token improves next-token prediction quality.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that the number of parameters and the amount of computation don’t have to grow together. Parameters give you a way to store knowledge, but computation determines how much work you can do with that knowledge on a particular problem.

Imagine giving a model the ability to revisit its internal representation, refine it, and perform several steps before producing an answer. You’re using the same parameters, but you’re allowing a more elaborate computation. For a difficult problem, that could be much more useful than simply making a single pass through a larger model.

The challenge is making that extra computation productive. Repeating the same operation doesn’t automatically lead to better reasoning. The model needs to learn how to use additional steps to make progress, and ideally how to allocate those steps depending on the input. A simple question shouldn’t require the same amount of work as a complicated mathematical problem.

So I see computation per parameter as another dimension of scaling. It could let us build models that are relatively compact in terms of what they store, but much more capable in terms of what they can do with it.

r001.rationale: The response does not compare LLMs’ cost efficiency with humans performing comparable tasks.

r002.rationale: It describes using the same parameters while revisiting and refining an internal representation over several computation steps, which frames added computation per parameter as internal thinking.

r003.rationale: It does not say that computation over past data before predicting a token improves next-token prediction quality; it discusses extra steps before producing an answer more generally.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that the number of parameters doesn’t tell you how much computation the model can actually do with what it knows. You can have a very large model, but if it has only a fixed amount of computation before producing the next token, that limits how much it can work through a difficult problem.

Increasing computation per parameter gives the model more opportunities to process information—to revisit intermediate results, refine a representation, or correct an initial mistake. Think of the difference between answering a question immediately and having time to work through it. You haven’t necessarily acquired more knowledge, but you can make better use of the knowledge you have.

The challenge is making that extra computation useful. Simply repeating the same operation doesn’t automatically produce better reasoning. You need an architecture and a training objective that teach the model how to use additional steps, and ideally how to allocate those steps depending on the difficulty of the input. So I would view it as another axis of scaling: not just how much knowledge a model can store, but how much work it can do with that knowledge.

r001.rationale: The response does not say current LLMs are cost-efficient compared with humans doing similar tasks.

r002.rationale: It describes extra computation as more opportunities to process information, revisit results, refine representations, and work through problems—an internal thinking process.

r003.rationale: It says extra computation before producing a token can help the model work through problems, but does not clearly state that computing over past data improves next-token prediction quality.
